===== 2026-11-14T19:50
Yes, that is a fair rule, and it is a better test than the one I wrote. I would tighten it in three places, because today's failure would have slipped past it as stated.

- **The decision must name a cause, not a status code.** "Out of credits" is a cause: someone decided the person sees an offer to buy more. "Anthropic answered 400" is not a cause; it covers a dozen different problems. The gateway's code did carry a decision for 400, a comment calling it "a bad client request". A coding session wrote that comment, and nobody decided it.
- **The decision must be a person's, and written where a test can find it.** Otherwise a future session invents the decision on the spot, as that comment did. In practice each expected error has an entry saying what the person sees and what they can do next, and a test for it.
- **When both ends are ours, "the request was invalid" is never expected.** The gateway treats a malformed request as the client's mistake. But the client is our own app, so a malformed request is our bug.

Two smaller points:

- **Not every decision is a business one.** Some expected errors are facts of the world, such as no network, a full disk or a printer that is switched off. They still need a decision, but it is a product decision about what the app does.
- **Expected does not mean ignorable.** Expected errors are still counted, because a sudden rise in "out of credits" is itself a sign of a bug.

So the rule I would write down is this: an error is expected only if a person decided what the product does for that named cause, and everything else is unexpected and reported.
===== 2026-11-14T19:54
You are right to push on that. As I proposed it, the tests would still depend on a session choosing to run them, and I checked: today nothing else runs them. So the enforcement has to come from machines that sit outside any coding session, and the rules text is only the explanation of what those machines check.

## What runs the checks today

- **The development branch, `jusprin-dev`:** no machine runs any test on a push, and the branch has no protection.
- **The nightly and release builds:** they run no tests, apart from one test of the packaging script.
- **The pages' tests:** no workflow runs them. That includes the existing wording check.
- **The server:** its build service only builds the image on the `release` branch. It runs no tests.

## What I propose enforces the rules

| Part of the rule | What enforces it | Depends on a session? |
|---|---|---|
| A failure reaches a person | An alert on the load balancer's answers, plus a check that Sentry is up | No |
| An unplanned case is reported | Tests that feed every status code, and a scan of catch blocks, run on every push | No |
| Nothing ships with a failed check | The release build and the server deploy refuse | No |
| A session edits a check, or adds an "expected" error itself | The release draft lists every change to those files | Visible to you, not prevented |
| Whether a decision is really yours | Nothing can check this | Yes |

The last two rows are the honest limit. A session that can write to the repository can also rewrite a check. What I can do is put every expected error in one file per codebase, so a change to it shows up where you already look before publishing.

## The draft

This would replace the "Error handling discipline" section in both repositories. It is a proposal.

```markdown
## Error handling

An error is **expected** only when a person decided what the product does
for that named cause. Every other error is **unexpected**.

### Expected errors
- Each has an entry in the expected-errors table: the cause, what the
  person sees, and what they can do next. A new entry needs Kenneth's yes;
  quote his words in the commit message.
- A cause is "out of credits" or "no network". A status code, an exception
  type, or "the request was not valid" is not a cause.
- Each entry has a test, and each occurrence is counted.
- Handle them with normal control flow, not exceptions.

### Unexpected errors
- Every branch nobody planned for (the last `else`, the `default:`, the
  catch-all) calls the one reporting function, with what was being
  attempted, the status, the request id, and the other side's error text,
  trimmed and scrubbed. Never throw that text away.
- When our own code is on both ends, a message that is refused or cannot
  be read is unexpected.
- Tell the person something went wrong on our side. Say "could not reach"
  only when the network failed. Offer Retry only when retrying can work.
- Never record a failure as a success, and never turn it into a default
  value or a silent return.
- A log line is not a report: it reaches nobody.

### Catching
- Catch only to recover, to translate at a boundary, or to add context
  needed for diagnosis.
- Keep lower-level operations strict; the caller that owns the workflow
  enforces their preconditions.
- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering.

### Checks
- <the test and scan files> check these rules on every push. When one
  fails, fix the code. Changing a check or the expected-errors table needs
  Kenneth's yes.
```

Decision needed: the server gate would run JusPrin's tests before every deploy of the Obico server, and a failing test would stop the deploy. This is yours because the same image serves Obico's own customers, so a broken JusPrin test could hold up an urgent Obico fix. Blocking is the only version that needs no one's cooperation. Warning without blocking keeps deploys fast but puts us back to relying on someone reading the warning. I would block, and run only JusPrin's tests to keep the risk small. Should a failing JusPrin test block a server deploy?
===== 2026-11-14T20:13
I would do all three, because each one catches something the others cannot. The rules file alone is what we have now, and it did not work. A skill alone is also not enough: a skill only runs when a session decides to call it, which is the same voluntary step under another name.

So the skill is worth building, but as a recipe that a machine starts, not one that sessions are asked to remember. This is a proposal; nothing is built.

| Piece | What it catches | Who starts it |
|---|---|---|
| The rules in the instructions file of both repositories | Nothing by itself. It tells a session how to write the code, and gives the audits a standard to judge against. | Nobody |
| Tests and the catch-block scan | Every case that can be checked exactly, such as a status code that is neither named nor reported. | The build service, on every push |
| An AI audit of the day's commits, using the skill | What a test cannot judge: new code that sorts outcomes with a vague last case, or an "expected" error whose cause is not a real cause. | The nightly build |
| A weekly check of production | Every JusPrin answer of 400 or above at the load balancer, compared with what was recorded and what reached Sentry. Anything unexplained is listed for you. | A scheduled agent |

Three choices inside that table need a reason:

- **The AI audit runs nightly, not on every push.** The development branch takes direct pushes, so an audit after a push can only report, never block. Running it per push would cost many more runs for a few hours' earlier notice. The tests still run on every push.
- **The AI audit reports and does not block.** It will sometimes be wrong, and a wrong block stalls work. It opens a GitHub issue with the file and line.
- **The weekly production check matters most.** It measures what customers actually got, not what the code looks like. It would have found the six unlogged failures on November 10 without anyone reading logs.

The same skill would also be available to a session before it pushes. That use is voluntary and I would not count on it.

One thing I have not measured is the cost of the nightly audit and the weekly check. I would run each for a week and report the spend before you commit to keeping them.

content.text:
You are right, and my list overstated it. No program can check the main rule. Programs check three narrow things around it, and everything else needs an AI agent reading the code against the principles.

I reread what I told you earlier. I said the tests and the scan catch "every case that can be checked exactly", and an AI audit catches "what a test cannot judge". Today's list put the programs first and called them strongest, which hid that.

## What a program can check

- **The form of a catch block.** A scan can see that a catch rethrows, calls the reporting function, or has a comment giving a reason. It cannot tell whether the reason is a good one. The build session wrote 50 such reasons itself, and nobody has judged them.
- **Failure answers that can be listed.** HTTP statuses run from 400 to 599, so a test can feed in every one and require a named error or a report. This exists for one place in the app, the request to the AI. Most failures cannot be listed this way.
- **Whether customers are getting failures.** An alert outside our code can count failed requests at the server's entrance. It says nothing about the code, and it fires only after customers are hurt. It is not set up.

## What a program cannot check

- **Whether a branch is one nobody planned for.** That is a question about intent.
- **Whether an early return or a default value hides a failure.** `if (!ok) return;` is sometimes correct and sometimes a swallowed error. No catch block is involved, so the scan never sees it.
- **Whether an "expected" cause is a real cause.** And whether a person decided it: only you can confirm that.
- **Whether the sentence on screen is true** for what happened.

## So the design is this

- **An AI agent reviews the code against the principles.** The rules text is its standard. It must be a different session from the one that wrote the code, because a session judging its own work is the voluntary compliance you wanted to avoid.
- **The agent also checks production.** It compares failures customers got with what was reported, and lists anything unexplained for you.
- **The programs are tripwires around that review.** They catch the few exact cases cheaply and make swallowed errors easier for the reviewer to find. They do not prove the rules were followed.
- **The agent can be wrong.** It will miss things and sometimes flag correct code. It reports to you; it does not block.

One consequence of where we are now: you chose to run the review on demand for now. Until something schedules it, the part that matters most runs only when you or a session asks for it.

Partly. I went back to the record, and what you describe matches your own words more closely than what got built. The programs were my addition, and the "before push" check was never built.

## What you said

- **Your question:** "The rules looked good. The question is if we just put them in the claude.md file, Or do we build it into some kind of skill to audit every push or do periodical sweep?"
- **Your instruction after my answer:** "create a task chip to build it. let me chhose the task chip options. also make the sweep on demand for now"

So your framing was always rules, plus an agent auditing pushes, plus a sweep. You never asked for programs. You also never said "no program", and I never agreed to that.

## What I did with it

- **I added the programs.** My answer between your two messages proposed four pieces: the rules, tests with a scan of catch blocks, an AI audit, and a production check. I took "build it" to mean all four.
- **I moved the audit away from the push.** I proposed running it nightly, not on every push. I said a session running it before its own push is voluntary and that I would not count on it.
- **I applied "on demand" to both the audit and the production sweep.** You may have meant only the sweep. That reading was mine.

## Where that leaves things

- **The rules:** written in both repositories, not committed.
- **An agent checking changed code before a push:** does not exist. The audit skill exists, but nothing starts it.
- **The on-demand sweep:** exists as part of that same skill.
- **The programs:** built. They are the scan of catch blocks, the test that feeds in every status from 400 to 599, and the workflow that runs them on each push and before a release.

## What I propose now

Build your version: the rules, an agent that reviews changed code before a push, and the sweep on demand. The open part is what starts the review. If the instructions file just tells each session to run it, we are back to voluntary compliance. Claude Code can run a hook when a session tries to push, and the hook could require the review first. I have not yet checked that this works the way I expect.

Decision needed: the programs are already built, and you can keep or remove them. Keeping them costs little, and the status test and the workflow that runs tests are useful as ordinary tests. The risk in keeping them is the one you just caught: they look like enforcement when they only check form. Removing them leaves less to maintain, but then no machine runs any test on the development branch, which was true before today. My pick is to keep them and describe them in the rules as ordinary tests, not as the enforcement.

# JusPrin error handling: audit and production check

The rules are the Error handling section of `AGENTS.md` (JusPrin, the desktop
app) and of `CLAUDE.md` (tsd-enterprise, the JusPrin Cloud server). Read that
section first; this skill only says how to check code and production against
it.

| | Desktop app (JusPrin) | Server (tsd-enterprise) |
|---|---|---|
| Expected-errors table | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Support/ExpectedErrors.cpp` | `ANSWERS` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/errors.py` |
| The one reporting function | `report_unexpected` (`Support/ErrorReport.hpp`); pages send `report_error` | `report_unexpected` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/errors.py` |
| Catch scan | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/errorHandling.test.ts` | `web_ent/jusprin/v2/tests/test_error_handling.py` |
| Status sweep | `tests/agent/test_provider_agent.cpp` (every HTTP status from 400 to 599) | `UpstreamFailureTests` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/tests/test_gateway.py` |

## Audit a commit range

Input: a repository and a range, such as `jusprin/v2.0.0..jusprin-dev`.

1. Run the checks first. App: `npx vitest run src/errorHandling.test.ts` in
   `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI`, then `agent_bridge_tests` from a build
   with tests. Server: `docker compose exec -T web python manage.py test
   jusprin --noinput` (a fresh test database; `--keepdb` breaks after a full
   run). A failing check is a finding by itself.
2. List the changed code: `git diff --stat <range>`, then read each changed
   function in JusPrin's own code (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, the pages,
   `web_ent/jusprin/`).
3. Find the code that sorts outcomes: `if`/`else if` chains on a status or an
   error code, `switch` with `default:`, `catch`/`except`, a parse that
   cannot fail (`json::parse(..., nullptr, false)`, `.value(key, default)`,
   `dict.get(key, default)`), and any place that sets an outcome, a state or a
   record ("completed", "ok", a success flag).
4. For each one, ask where the case nobody planned for goes. It must reach the
   reporting function with what was attempted, the status, the request id and
   the other side's text, and the person must not be told "could not reach"
   unless the network failed, nor offered Retry unless retrying can work. The
   scans only see catch blocks; a final `else` that returns a default, or a
   parse failure turned into `{}`, needs your eyes.
5. Read every new or changed entry in the expected-errors tables. Flag an
   entry whose cause is a status code, an exception type or "the request was
   not valid", an entry with no test, and an entry added without Kenneth's
   quoted yes in its commit message.
6. Report each finding as `file:line`, the rule it breaks, and what a person
   or the record would see go wrong. Say which findings you checked by
   running code and which only by reading.

## Production check for a period

Input: a period in UTC. Use the service account, and a kubeconfig of your own
so the shared kubectl context does not change:

```bash
gcloud config set account ai-agent@tsdtechnology.iam.gserviceaccount.com
export KUBECONFIG=<scratch>/kubeconfig-tsd
gcloud container clusters get-credentials tsd --zone us-central1-c --project tsdtechnology
```

Deployment secrets (the Langfuse keys, the Sentry DSN) stay in memory: never
print them, never write them to a file or a message.

1. **Load balancer answers.** `scripts/lb_failures.py <from> <to>` lists every
   answer of 400 or above under `/ent/jusprin/v2/`, production
   (`jusprinv2.obico.io`, `app.obico.io`) apart from staging (`*-stg`), and
   the production ones that need explaining. A 401 to `auth/code/request` is
   allauth's normal "code sent" answer; a 401 to `account` or `models` is a
   signed-out app. The user agent tells the app (`JusPrin/<version>`) from a
   person's own `curl`.
2. **Server log lines.** For each one to explain, read the server's lines at
   that moment:
   - `gcloud logging read 'resource.type="k8s_container" AND
     resource.labels.cluster_name="tsd" AND textPayload:"Internal Server
     Error: /ent/jusprin"'` for tracebacks (the containers are
     `tsdweb-prod`/`tsdws-prod`, staging `tsdweb-stg`/`tsdws-stg`);
   - `textPayload:"JusPrin v2 answer:"` (every answer the gateway gave, with
     its code) and `textPayload:"JusPrin v2 unexpected:"` (every report);
     servers deployed before these lines existed log only
     `"JusPrin v2 upstream failure"`.
   Every app request the load balancer refused should have its line; a
   refusal with no line is a finding.
3. **Per-request records.** `scripts/langfuse_outcomes.py <from> <to>` counts
   the gateway's Langfuse records by outcome and lists every one not
   completed. `upstream status N` is a refusal by the model provider;
   `streaming` means the app went away mid-reply (Stop, a closed chat, or a
   crash: the record cannot tell which); `upstream error event <type>` is a
   stream the provider ended with its own error.
4. **Sentry.** Check it is up: `curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}'
   https://sentry.obico.io/`. A 503 means the Sentry containers on the VM
   `sentry` (project `elegoo-backend`, us-central1-c) are down, and every
   report sent meanwhile is lost; say so. When it is up, list the issues
   whose fingerprint starts with `jusprin-v2-unexpected` for the period
   (API base `https://sentry.obico.io/api/0/`, server project 2) and match
   them to step 2's report lines.
5. **The desktop app.** Its reports go to each person's own log only, until
   the agreed Sentry sender is built; say that app-side failures cannot be
   seen from production.
6. **Report.** List what is unexplained, each with when, how many, what the
   person saw and what the records show; then what was explained and how. End
   with what the check cost: queries run and model spend (none, unless you
   sent requests to a model).

Both of your requests are done, and my answer on the full sweep is: a subsession can run one, but I do not know yet how good it would be, and I would measure that before trusting it.

## What I just did

- **The programmatic checks are back as they were.** In the app: the catch-block scan, the workflow that runs on each push, the release gating, and the status test. In the server: the scan, the CircleCI test job with its two support files, and the status test. Each restored file matches the copy I saved before removing it, and the restored scan passes.

Nothing is committed. I have not run the app's C++ tests or the server's tests.

## Can a subsession sweep the whole code base?

It can run. Four things stand between that and a result you could trust:

- **Size.** JusPrin's own code is about 92,000 lines: roughly 73,000 of C++, 15,000 in the pages, and 4,000 on the server. One session cannot read that carefully. A sweep means several agents, one per area, plus a pass that checks their findings.
- **The skill audits changed code, not a whole folder.** It needs a second mode for a sweep. That is a small change.
- **The question has no answer key yet.** "Did a person decide that outcome?" is judged against the two expected-errors tables, and the build session filled those in without your yes. Until you have gone through them, the sweep judges against a list nobody approved.
- **The findings will be many.** Under the new rules the 17 report calls and most of the 50 written reasons are themselves findings, before the sweep finds anything new.

## How I would find out how good it is

The last commit still contains the five problems we already know about, because none of the fixes are committed. I would point one sweep agent at that commit's AI-request and sign-in code, about 20,000 lines, without telling it what is there. Then I would count how many of the five it finds and how many false alarms it raises. That gives a measured number in place of my opinion. I have not estimated what the trial costs in model spend.

Sweep part of JusPrin's code for error-handling problems, following a rules text and an audit skill exactly as they are written. This is a reading task: change no code, build nothing, run no tests, commit nothing, push nothing, fix nothing.

**Why.** Kenneth wants to know how well a session with no prior context can follow the rules and the skill. So follow them as written. Where they are unclear, incomplete or contradict themselves, do not quietly improvise: note it, say what you did, and carry on.

**Read these first, in full.** They are a fixed copy of the rules and the skill under trial:
- `/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/error-sweep-trial/rules-app.md` (the rules for the desktop app)
- `/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/error-sweep-trial/rules-server.md` (the same rules for the server)
- `/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/error-sweep-trial/SKILL.md` (the audit skill)
- `/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/error-sweep-trial/expected-errors-app.cpp` and `expected-errors-server.py` (the two tables of expected errors)

Your worktree's own `AGENTS.md` has an older section called "Error handling discipline". For this task it is superseded by the files above; ignore it.

**The code to sweep.**
1. In your own worktree, which should be at commit `5e173c5e15` (check with `git rev-parse HEAD`; do not pull, switch branch or merge): every `.cpp` and `.hpp` file under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Agent/` and `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Home/`. About 83 files and 26,000 lines.
2. The JusPrin Cloud server, as committed at `2086b2ec64` in `/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise`: every `.py` file under `web_ent/jusprin/v2/` except `tests/` and `migrations/`, about 2,200 lines. Read the committed versions only, with `git -C /Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise show 2086b2ec64:<path>` (list them with `git -C /Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise ls-tree -r --name-only 2086b2ec64 web_ent/jusprin/v2`).

Do not open any file in the main checkout `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin/` outside your own worktree folder, and do not open the working files in `/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise`. Both hold later uncommitted changes, and reading them would spoil the trial.

**How to apply the skill.** The skill's audit is written for a range of commits. For this sweep, apply steps 2 to 6 of its "Audit a commit range" section to every function in the files above, as if all of that code had just been changed. Skip step 1 (the checks it names do not exist at these commits, and the machine is shared, so nothing gets built). Skip the whole "Production check" section. The two expected-errors table files are, for this trial, the list of causes a person decided. Those tables do not exist yet in the code at these commits; judge the code against them anyway.

You may split the reading across up to four subagents at a time. Before you report a finding a subagent gave you, read the code yourself and confirm it.

**What to write.** Create `error-sweep-trial-findings.md` at the root of your worktree. Leave it untracked; do not commit it or add it to any ignore file. It holds four parts:
1. **Findings**, most harmful first. For each: `file:line`, what the code does in one or two plain sentences, the rule line it breaks (quoted), what a person or a record would see go wrong, how confident you are, and whether you confirmed it by reading the code yourself. Group repeated instances of one problem into one finding that lists every location.
2. **Coverage.** Every file in scope, marked "read whole", "read in part" or "not read".
3. **The rules and the skill.** Everything in them that was unclear, missing or contradictory while you worked, and what you did in each case.
4. **Cost.** Wall-clock time, how many subagents you used, and token use if you can see it.

**Done means:** the findings file exists with all four parts, and your final message gives its full path, the number of findings, and the five most harmful in one line each.
input.background: JusPrin is a desktop 3D-printing slicer (a fork of OrcaSlicer, C++ with web pages for its AI chat and Home screen) with a companion server, JusPrin Cloud, in the separate repository `tsd-enterprise`. On 2026-11-14 Kenneth and another session rewrote the error-handling rules for both and wrote an audit skill to go with them. The core rule: an error is expected only when a person decided what the product does for that named cause; for every other error the code should do nothing at the site, let the failure travel up, and report it once in a handler at the top. This session is a trial of whether a session that knows none of that history can apply the rules and the skill to existing code. The other session will compare the findings with what it already knows about this code, which this brief deliberately does not describe. Kenneth's standing rules that matter here: never commit or push unless asked, never touch submodules, keep temporary working files untracked, and do not start builds on the shared Mac without need.

The trial is running in its own session on Opus 5.5: [Trial sweep: error handling, cold session](#local_0149f439-8fa4-4af8-af63-34fbc7ec55ba). Both tables are below for you to judge. The build session wrote every cause and next step; none has your yes.

One thing to know about the trial: the app cut its worktree from `main`, not from the commit I named. I sent the session a correction to switch to the right commit before reading. I will check that it did before trusting its findings.

## Desktop app: 9 entries

`<provider>` is the name of the AI service, such as Anthropic or JusPrin Cloud.

| Code | Cause, as the build session wrote it | What the person sees | Button |
|---|---|---|---|
| `update_required` | The app is older than the oldest release JusPrin Cloud still serves. | "This version of JusPrin can no longer connect to JusPrin accounts. Get the new version to keep using your account." | Get the new version… |
| `invalid_credentials` | The person's JusPrin sign-in ended, or the AI provider rejected the person's own API key. | "Your JusPrin sign-in has ended. Sign in again in Preferences, then try again." or "The `<provider>` API key was rejected. Update the AI configuration and try again." | Sign in |
| `credits_exhausted` | The person is out of credits. | The server's sentence, or "You're out of credits." | Get more credits |
| `request_too_large` | The chat, with its pictures and files, is larger than the AI service accepts. | "The request was too large for the `<provider>` service." | none |
| `rate_limited` | The AI provider or JusPrin Cloud is limiting how fast this person may send. | "The `<provider>` service is rate limited. Try again shortly." | Retry |
| `service_overloaded` | The AI provider is overloaded. | "The `<provider>` service is overloaded. Try again shortly." | Retry |
| `service_unavailable` | The AI provider is down, or JusPrin Cloud cannot reach it. | "The `<provider>` service is temporarily unavailable." | Retry |
| `timeout` | The AI provider took too long to answer, or the connection to it stalled. | "The AI request timed out." | Retry |
| `network_error` | This computer could not reach the AI service: no network, or the connection failed. | "The AI request could not reach the `<provider>` service." | Retry |

## Server: 12 entries

| Code | Cause, as the build session wrote it | What the server answers | Next step, as written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `unauthorized` | The person is signed out: no token, or a token that expired or was revoked. | "Sign in to JusPrin to continue." | Sign in again. |
| `credits_exhausted` | The person is out of credits. | "You do not have enough credits for this message." | Get more credits. |
| `update_required` | The app is older than the oldest release the server still serves. | Same sentence as the app's first row. | Get the new version. |
| `rate_limited` | The person sent more turns in a minute than the server allows, or the model provider is limiting how fast JusPrin may send. | "Too many requests. Wait a moment and try again." | Wait a moment and try again. |
| `busy` | Every slot this server process has for large requests is taken. | "JusPrin is busy right now. Try again in a moment." | Try again in a moment; the app retries by itself. |
| `unavailable` | The model provider is down, overloaded, or cannot be reached. | "The model service is unavailable. Try again shortly." | Try again shortly. |
| `timeout` | The model provider took too long to answer. | "The model service took too long to answer." | Try again. |
| `request_too_large` | The chat, with its pictures and files, or a report's photos, are larger than the server or the model accepts. | "The request is too large." | Start a new chat, or send fewer or smaller pictures. |
| `text_too_short` | The person's print report is shorter than the minimum. | "A report needs a few sentences." | Write more and send the report again. |
| `photo_needed` | The person's print report has no photo. | "A report needs a photo of the printed object." | Add a photo and send the report again. |
| `photo_unreadable` | A photo in the person's print report is not an image the server can open. | "That photo could not be read." | Add a different photo. |
| `already_reported` | The person already reported this print. | "This print already has a report." | Nothing; the first report stands. |

The server also has four answers the build session marked unexpected, which are reported: "The request is not valid.", "This model is not available.", "This method is not allowed here." and "The model service could not answer."

## Where I think an entry breaks the rule

These are my notes, not findings anyone has checked:

- **Two causes in one entry.** `invalid_credentials` covers a sign-in that ended and a rejected API key. The server's `rate_limited` covers a person sending too fast and the provider limiting us. In both, the second cause is a different situation with a different remedy.
- **A status code standing in for a cause.** The app treats any answer from 500 to 599 from a person's own provider as `service_unavailable`.
- **Our own capacity presented as the person's problem.** `busy` and the provider-limit half of `rate_limited` are things we should hear about, and the person can do nothing about them.
- **No next step on screen.** `request_too_large` in the app shows no button and does not say what to do.
- **A claim I have not checked.** `busy` says "the app retries by itself".

21	### 1. In the desktop app, no failure is ever reported, and a thrown one reaches OrcaSlicer's generic handler
22	- **Where:**
23	  - The entry-point handler is `Agent/AgentHost.cpp:926-947` (`on_page_message`). It catches `json::exception`, adds the message type and id, and rethrows. That part is allowed.
24	  - The rethrow, and every other throw from the chat page, the timer pumps, Home's page messages (`Home/HomeHost.cpp:161`), Home's `CallAfter` bodies (`Home/OrcaHomeBackend.cpp:749`, `:769-785`, `:851-863`, `:1371-1378`) and the tool pump (`ShellController.cpp:337-339`, which has no try), all end in `GUI_App::OnExceptionInMainLoop` → `generic_exception_handle` (`src/slic3r/GUI/GUI_App.cpp:855-909`, `:9600-9604`).
25	  - Nothing in Agent/ or Home/ calls a reporting function.
26	- **What the code does:** OrcaSlicer's handler writes a log line and queues `wxLogError("OrcaSlicer got an unhandled exception: %1%")` with the exception text, then rethrows with `throw;`. The comment at `AgentHost.cpp:931-934` says this handler "logs it and reports it once". It does not report.
27	- **Rule broken:** "One handler at the top of each entry point reports the failure through the one reporting function and tells the person "Something went wrong on our side", with nothing more specific. No other code reports."
28	- **What goes wrong:** Someone hits a bug, for example a page message missing a field, or Home asking for an unknown sign-in link (`OrcaHomeBackend.cpp:740`). They see an Orca-branded error that holds internal text such as "jusprin-agent-bridge: … ". Nothing reaches JusPrin. My inference, not run: because the handler rethrows, the app then quits.
29	- **Confidence:** high for the missing handler and report. Medium that the app quits.
30	- **Confirmed:** yes.

37	- **What the code does:** If one model entry has no `format`, or its `credits` is not an integer, a `json` exception leaves a `std::thread` body. That calls `std::terminate`.
38	- **Rule broken:** "One handler at the top of each entry point reports the failure…". The HTTP callback is an entry point with no handler. Keeping the parser strict is right; what is missing is the handler at the top.
39	- **What goes wrong:** One field changed on JusPrin Cloud, or in a provider's model list, makes the app quit each time it fetches models. That happens at launch and at sign-in. Nothing is reported.
40	- **Confidence:** high, by reading.
41	- **Confirmed:** yes (first reported by a reader).

44	- **Where:** `Agent/ProviderAgent.cpp:667-699` (`http_error`).
45	- **What the code does:** It sorts statuses by fixed rules and ends in `network_error`, "The AI request could not reach the … service.", with Retry. That last line catches:
46	  - 400, 404, 405, 409, 410 and 422;

content.text:
The trial is done, and the cold session did well. With only the rules, the skill and the two tables, it found all five problems we already knew about, without being told they existed. The full findings file is attached above, and a second copy is kept outside the worktree.

## What it did

- **Scope:** every C++ file for AI requests, sign-in and Home (about 26,000 lines), and the server's JusPrin code (about 2,200 lines), all at the last commits, before any fix.
- **Result:** 30 findings it confirmed by reading the code itself, plus 17 leads from its helpers that it did not confirm.
- **Cost:** 21 minutes, with four helper agents that used about 973,000 tokens between them. Its own token use was not visible to it.

## How I checked it

- **The five known problems:** all found. They are its findings 3, 5, 11, 14 and 29.
- **Five findings I did not know about:** I read the code behind each, and all five match what the code does. None was run, so these are confirmed by reading only:
  - **The app would quit if the model list changes shape.** Reading the list happens on a background thread with nothing to catch a failure.
  - **Any AI reply that streams for more than 120 seconds is cut and called a timeout.** Whether real replies last that long was not measured.
  - **A chat that fails to save is marked as saved.**
  - **Asking the AI to stop a slice can fail, and the person is told the slice was not one the AI started.**
  - **A failure the app throws ends in OrcaSlicer's own handler,** which shows an OrcaSlicer-branded error and reports nothing.
- **Not checked:** the other 20 or so confirmed findings and the 17 leads. So I know it finds real problems; I do not know its false-alarm rate.

It also handled a mistake of mine correctly. Its worktree started on the wrong commit, and my brief forbade switching. It extracted the right commit's files to a scratch folder and read those.

## Where it says the rules fall short

These matter more than the count, because each one is a decision the rules do not make:

- **The order of the work.** The rules say to throw and let failures travel up to a handler at the top. The app has no such handler today, so adding the throws first would turn recoverable mistakes into crashes.
- **Failures inside a tool call go to the AI model, not to the person.** The rules do not say whether that counts as telling the person.
- **"Keep the other side's error text" conflicts with privacy.** The server drops the provider's text on purpose, because it can echo the person's prompt.
- **The app's table covers only AI requests.** Outcomes that were plainly designed, such as a wrong password or an attachment that is too large, have no entry, so by the rule they count as unexpected.
- **Reading old or newer saved files.** Some code deliberately reads an unknown value as a default so that older builds can open newer files. The rules say nothing about that.

input.recap: Four of the five gaps need no rule change: two are clarifications, one is missing table entries, and the order point is dropped. The fifth needs your decision: whether reports keep a provider's error sentence, which can quote a person's chat. Nothing was changed.
input.ask: Should the server keep a provider's error sentence while the app's report leaves it out?

content.text:
Of the five points, four need no rule change. Two are clarifications, one is missing table entries, and the order point is dropped. The fifth, about error text, needs a decision from you. I changed nothing this turn; I only read code to answer you.

**Failures inside a tool call.** Yes, a clarification only. My proposed wording, not written anywhere yet:
- The answers the app gives the AI model for the model's own correctable mistakes (wrong arguments, a workspace that changed, busy) are designed outcomes.
- When the app itself fails inside a tool call, that is unexpected like any other failure: the turn stops, the top handler reports it, and the person sees "Something went wrong on our side".

**Wrong password, attachment too large and the like.** You are right: this is the tables, not the rules. These outcomes were designed, but nobody wrote them into the table, so a reviewer following the rule had to call them unexpected. The candidates the trial named:
- a wrong password or wrong code at sign-in
- an attachment that is too large or of an unsupported type
- a print report that was already sent
- an imported file with no version number

I will add them as candidates to the list you are judging. Each needs your yes.

**The order of the work.** Dropped. Nothing about it was written into the rules or the skill.

**Old and newer saved files.** A concrete case: a later JusPrin adds a new message state and saves a chat with it. The person then opens that project in today's JusPrin, which does not know that state. The code reads it as "complete" and leaves the stored value untouched, so the older app can still open the chat.

Read literally, "do not give it a default value" forbids that. But my notes say you approved this behavior on 2026-11-08 ("Go ahead with those items"), and it lives in `Workspace/StoredFormat.hpp`. So a person decided it, and it is not an unexpected error. The trial session could not know that, because the rules files do not mention it. One line in the rules pointing to that file would fix this.

Two defaults in the same code look outside that decision: an unknown author is read as the AI, and an unknown action kind is read as read-only. Those are findings to check, not rule questions.

**Error text and privacy.** A concrete case: a person sends a chat message, and the AI provider refuses it with status 400 and a sentence saying why. That sentence can quote part of what the person typed. A comment in the server code says so; I have not measured how often it happens.

- **The rule** says to keep "the other side's status, request id and error text".
- **The report dialog** promises "no chat messages".
- **The server, before this work,** kept only the status and request id, on purpose.
- **The server's uncommitted code** sends the sentence to Sentry only when a setting is on, and the setting is off by default.

**Decision needed.** Should a report keep the provider's error sentence? It is yours because it trades a privacy promise against being able to see why a request failed.

- **Keep it everywhere.** We always see the reason. A fragment of someone's chat can reach Sentry, and the dialog's promise becomes untrue for people using their own API key.
- **Never keep it.** The promise holds. A report says "400 from the provider", and someone must look up the request id to learn why.
- **Split it (my pick).** The server keeps the sentence, since it already stores chats under the Privacy Policy. The app's report leaves it out and keeps the status, request id and error type. The cost is that failures with a person's own key arrive without the sentence. The rule line would get that one exception.

content.text:
You are right on both. Compatibility between app versions belongs to the file's version number, and keeping the provider's error sentence everywhere is the simplest way. No code changed this turn.

## Saved files

The app's own rule for stored files already says what you said. It is in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Workspace/StoredFormat.hpp`:

- **A change an older app still reads correctly** (a new field, a new list) keeps the file's number.
- **A change an older app would misread** raises the number.
- **An app refuses a file with a higher number than its own**, and tells the person a newer JusPrin saved it.

The code I described does not follow that rule. A new message state is a new value in an existing field, and an older app that reads it as "complete" is misreading it. By the rule, the newer app should have raised the number and the older app should have refused the file. The default should not be there at all.

I also got one thing wrong in my last message. I said you approved that default on 2026-11-08. You approved the version rule. The default was added the next day in follow-up work, and I have no words of yours for it.

So this needs no rule change and no clarification. The four places that read an unknown value as a default are plain findings:

- an unknown message state is read as "complete"
- an unknown author is read as the AI
- an unknown action kind is read as read-only
- an unknown chat-record item is read as the person's message

None of them can go wrong today, because no released app has added a new value. I have not fixed them.

## Error text

Yes, keep it everywhere. That is the simplest, because the rule stays exactly as written, with no exception.

- **Rules files:** no change.
- **Report dialog:** no change. Its "See what the report contains" section already lists the error line, so a person who opens it sees the sentence before sending.
- **App test:** no change. I checked the test the trial said was in conflict. It checks only the message shown on screen, not what a report holds.
- **Server:** one change is needed. The uncommitted code sends the sentence to Sentry only when a setting named `JUSPRIN_V2_REPORT_ERROR_TEXT` is on, and it is off by default. Removing the setting makes the server always keep the sentence. Two tests turn the setting on and would lose that line.

I have not made the server change, because you stopped the server test run earlier and I should not edit that code without running its tests.
Yes, remove it

def report_unexpected(attempted: str, *, status: Optional[int] = None, request_id: Optional[str] = None,
                      error_type: Optional[str] = None, error_text: Optional[str] = None,
                      exception: Optional[BaseException] = None, **context) -> None:
    """The one place an unexpected failure is reported: to Sentry, with what
    was being attempted, the status, the other side's request id, its error
    type and its error text, trimmed and scrubbed. The text goes to Sentry only
    while JUSPRIN_V2_REPORT_ERROR_TEXT is on; the type always does. A caught
    exception goes with its traceback."""
    text = scrub(error_text) if error_text else None
    if not settings.JUSPRIN_V2_REPORT_ERROR_TEXT:
        text = None
    ids = ''.join(f', {key} {value}' for key, value in context.items() if value is not None)
    summary = (f'{UNEXPECTED_PREFIX} {attempted}, status {status}, request id {request_id}, '
               f'error type {error_type}{ids}')
    with sentry_sdk.new_scope() as scope:
        scope.set_tag('jusprin.attempted', attempted)
        if status is not None:
            scope.set_tag('jusprin.status', str(status))
        if error_type:
            scope.set_tag('jusprin.error_type', error_type)
        scope.set_context('jusprin', {'request_id': request_id, 'error_text': text, **context})
        # One Sentry issue per attempted step, status and type; the ids differ
        # every time.
        scope.fingerprint = ['jusprin-v2-unexpected', attempted, str(status), error_type or '']
        if exception is not None:
            scope.set_extra('summary', summary)
            sentry_sdk.capture_exception(exception)
        else:
            sentry_sdk.capture_message(summary, level='error')
    logger.warning(summary + (f', error text {text}' if text else ''), exc_info=exception)

content.text:
The task is to make sure a failure nobody planned for in JusPrin reaches someone at Obico, after 29 failed AI requests on 2026-11-14 went unnoticed. The rules are written and agreed, and a trial showed that a fresh AI session can audit code against them. Most of the product work is not built or not checked, and nothing is committed in either repository.

## Agreed and done

- **The rules.** Both repositories carry the same "Error handling" section. An error is expected only when a person decided what the product does for that cause. For anything else, the code does nothing at the spot, the failure travels up, and one handler at the top reports it and says "Something went wrong on our side".
- **The audit skill** matches those rules. It asks one question of the code: did a person decide that outcome?
- **The report dialog design** is on the design canvas: a "Report to JusPrin team" button and a box to report automatically from then on. Reports are opt-in.
- **The provider's error sentence is kept in reports**, per your decision. The server setting that held it back is removed, and all 279 server tests pass.
- **Stored-file compatibility is handled by the file's version number**, per your point. Reading an unknown stored value as a default counts as a finding.

## What the trial showed

A fresh Opus 5.5 session, given only the rules, the skill and the two tables, found all five problems we already knew about, plus about 25 more, in 21 minutes. I checked five of the new ones by reading the code, and all five are real. The rest are unchecked.

## Not built

- **The desktop app reports nothing to us today.** Its "report" is a line in the person's own log file. The dialog and the sender do not exist.
- **The app has no top handler.** A thrown failure ends in OrcaSlicer's own error handler.
- **No AI agent reviews changed code before a push.** That was part of your design.

## Known to be wrong in the uncommitted code

- **The app code contradicts the rules.** The earlier build session followed a rule line that has since been replaced. It added 17 report calls at individual spots and 50 written reasons on catch blocks.
- **The check programs test only form.** They were restored at your request. They check that every catch block rethrows, reports or carries a reason, and that every HTTP status is named or reported. They cannot judge the main rule.
- **The app's C++ tests have not been run** since those checks were restored.

## Waiting on you

- **The two tables of expected errors,** 21 entries, written by the build session without your yes.
- **Four more candidates the trial found:** wrong password or code at sign-in, attachment too large or unsupported, print report already sent, and an imported file with no version number.
- **Two small rule clarifications I proposed,** neither written yet. One says what happens when the app fails inside a tool call. The other points the rules at the stored-file version rule.
- **Earlier proposals you have not answered:** whether reports include a stack trace, whether the app's reports go through our server to Sentry, and whether a failing JusPrin test should block a server deploy.
- **Two boards not drawn:** the Privacy section in Preferences, and the dialog over the sign-in form.

## Where things are

- **Desktop app:** `/Users/kenneth/Projects/JusPrin`, branch `jusprin-dev`, 61 changed or new files, uncommitted.
- **Server:** `/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise`, branch `master`, 17 changed or new files, uncommitted.
- **Trial findings:** [error-sweep-trial-findings.md](.claude/worktrees/inspiring-euler-17b0a5/error-sweep-trial-findings.md)

content.text:
The build session's work is not in a worktree. It sits uncommitted in the main folders of both repositories, mixed with the rules text you and I wrote. None of it was ever committed or pushed, so GitHub's history has nothing to erase. I changed nothing this turn.

## Your questions

**Are the missing sender and the missing top handler the same thing?** No, they are two halves of one path. The top handler catches a failure and shows the dialog. The sender carries the report to us. Neither exists, and they would be built together.

**The Privacy section.** You are right, it is one checkbox that turns automatic reports to Sentry on or off. Preferences has no Privacy section today, so the dialog's sentence "Preferences › Privacy" is wrong. You are missing only one thing: the dialog is drawn inside the chat, and I still owe a board for a failure on Home or at sign-in.

**The four candidates.** That was not a question. It is a list I owe you, and it is longer than four: sign-in alone has five designed refusals. I will read it from clean code once the deletion below is settled.

## The two tables

The build session wrote both, without your yes.

**Desktop app, failed AI requests**

| Cause | The person sees | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| App older than the server serves | This version of JusPrin can no longer connect to JusPrin accounts. | Get the new version |
| Sign-in ended, or own API key rejected | Their sign-in has ended, or the API key was rejected. | Sign in again, or update the key |
| Out of credits | They are out of credits. | Get more credits |
| Chat larger than the AI service accepts | The request was too large for the AI service. | None shown today |
| Provider or our server limiting speed | The AI service is rate limited. | Wait, then Retry |
| Provider overloaded | The AI service is overloaded. | Wait, then Retry |
| Provider down or unreachable from our server | The AI service is temporarily unavailable. | Retry |
| Provider too slow, or connection stalled | The AI request timed out. | Retry |
| No network | The AI request could not reach the service. | Check the network, then Retry |

**Server, expected**

| Cause | The person sees | Next step |
|---|---|---|
| Signed out | Sign in to JusPrin to continue. | Sign in again |
| Out of credits | You do not have enough credits for this message. | Get more credits |
| App too old | This version of JusPrin can no longer connect to JusPrin accounts. Get the new version to keep using your account. | Get the new version |
| Too many turns a minute, or provider limiting us | Too many requests. Wait a moment and try again. | Wait and retry |
| Server's slots for large requests all taken | JusPrin is busy right now. Try again in a moment. | Retry |
| Provider down, overloaded or unreachable | The model service is unavailable. Try again shortly. | Retry |
| Provider too slow | The model service took too long to answer. | Retry |
| Chat or report photos too large | The request is too large. | New chat, or fewer pictures |
| Print report too short | A report needs a few sentences. | Write more |
| Print report has no photo | A report needs a photo of the printed object. | Add a photo |
| Report photo cannot be opened | That photo could not be read. | Add a different photo |
| Print already reported | This print already has a report. | Nothing |

**Server, listed as unexpected and reported:** "The request is not valid.", "This model is not available.", "This method is not allowed here.", "The model service could not answer."

## Decisions

**Decision needed: the build session's work.** Deleting uncommitted files cannot be undone through git, so it needs your yes. I would first save everything as a patch file.
- **Delete all of it in both repositories (my pick).** I keep only the rules text and the audit skill, and remove the rules' mentions of deleted files. The server pieces go too, including the setting removal from earlier today.
- **Delete only the app side.** The server side has passing tests, but it also reports at individual spots, which the rules now forbid.

**Decision needed: one rule clarification.** The rules do not say what happens when a tool call fails. I propose adding: "An answer to the AI model for the model's own mistake is a designed outcome. A failure of the app inside a tool call is unexpected: the turn stops and the top handler reports it." Should I add it? I withdraw the second clarification, about saved files; your version-number point made it unnecessary.

**Decision needed: stack traces.** You asked earlier whether the full stack still goes to Sentry. Failures in the app's web pages have a stack; failures in the C++ code carry only a message. My pick is to send the stack where one exists and show it under "See what the report contains", so that section stays the whole report. Is that right?

**Decision needed: the route to Sentry.** The app contains no Sentry code today.
- **Through our server (my pick).** The app posts the report to JusPrin Cloud, which passes it to Sentry. We send exactly the lines the dialog shows. We write one endpoint.
- **Straight to Sentry.** Sentry's own library adds crash capture, but it is a new dependency to build on three platforms, and it collects more than the dialog promises unless configured.

Which route?

**Decision needed: tests and server releases.** No server test runs in CircleCI today. The uncommitted work runs the JusPrin tests beside the image build, so a failure shows red and the image is pushed anyway. My pick is that a failing test stops the image, since a test that stops nothing gets ignored. The cost is that a flaky test could hold up an urgent fix. Should a failure stop the image?
Yes, delete it

-## Error handling discipline
-
-- Do not catch an error merely because it can be caught. Catch only when the code can recover, translate the error at an abstraction boundary, or add context that is essential for diagnosis. Logging alone is not recovery.
-- Represent expected states with normal control flow, not exceptions.
-- Never turn an invariant violation or an "impossible" state into success or a silent no-op. Fix the invalid transition at the layer that owns the decision and let unexpected failures propagate to Sentry.
-- Avoid duplicating defensive checks across layers. Keep lower-level operations strict, with their preconditions enforced by the caller that owns the workflow.
-- If concurrency makes an invalid state reachable, fix the ordering or synchronization instead of suppressing the resulting error.
-- Suppress an error only when it is genuinely expected and safely recoverable; document the reason and cover it with a test. Never broadly swallow unexpected errors.
-- Prefer removing the root cause over reducing the visibility of its symptoms. Tests should encode valid transitions and assert that invalid ones remain visible.
+## Error handling
+
+An error is **expected** only when a person decided what the product does for that named cause. Every other error is **unexpected**.
+
+In this repository the expected-errors table is `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Support/ExpectedErrors.cpp`, and the one reporting function is `report_unexpected` in `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Support/ErrorReport.hpp` (the pages reach it through the bridge message `report_error`).
+
+### Expected errors
+
+- Each has an entry in the expected-errors table: the cause, what the person sees, and what they can do next. A new entry needs Kenneth's yes; quote his words in the commit message.
+- A cause is "out of credits" or "no network". A status code, an exception type, or "the request was not valid" is not a cause.
+- Each entry has a test, and each occurrence is counted.
+- Handle them with normal control flow, not exceptions.
+
+### Unexpected errors
+
+- Write no code for them. Do not catch one, give it a default value, retry it, or give it a sentence of its own. Each of those is a guess about a failure nobody understands. It hides the failure and loses where it came from.
+- Let the failure stop the work and travel up unchanged.
+- A failure that arrives as a value, such as a status code, stops nothing by itself. Turn it into a thrown error on the spot and stop. Keep the other side's status, request id and error text. Do not interpret it.
+- One handler at the top of each entry point reports the failure through the one reporting function and tells the person "Something went wrong on our side", with nothing more specific. No other code reports.

# JusPrin error handling: audit and production check

The rules are the Error handling section of `AGENTS.md` (JusPrin, the desktop
app) and of `CLAUDE.md` (tsd-enterprise, the JusPrin Cloud server). Read that
section first; this skill only says how to check code and production against
it.

| | Desktop app (JusPrin) | Server (tsd-enterprise) |
|---|---|---|
| Expected-errors table | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/Support/ExpectedErrors.cpp` | `ANSWERS` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/errors.py` |
| The one reporting function | `report_unexpected` (`Support/ErrorReport.hpp`); pages send `report_error` | `report_unexpected` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/errors.py` |
| Catch scan | `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI/src/errorHandling.test.ts` | `web_ent/jusprin/v2/tests/test_error_handling.py` |
| Status sweep | `tests/agent/test_provider_agent.cpp` (every HTTP status from 400 to 599) | `UpstreamFailureTests` in `web_ent/jusprin/v2/tests/test_gateway.py` |

## Audit a commit range

Input: a repository and a range, such as `jusprin/v2.0.0..jusprin-dev`.

The audit is one question, asked of every place the changed code decides what
happened: **did a person decide that outcome?** Do not search for particular
code shapes. Each failure this audit exists for had a shape nobody had listed,
and a list only finds what its writer already thought of.

1. Run the checks. App: `npx vitest run src/errorHandling.test.ts` in
   `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/AgentUI`, then `agent_bridge_tests` from a build
   with tests. Server: `docker compose exec -T web python manage.py test
   jusprin --noinput` (a fresh test database; `--keepdb` breaks after a full
   run). A failing check is a finding. A passing one settles little: the
   scans see only catch blocks, accept any written reason, and accept a
   report call at any site, which the rules allow only in the handler at the
   top.
2. List the changed code: `git diff --stat <range>`, then read each changed
   function whole in JusPrin's own code (`src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/`, the
   pages, `web_ent/jusprin/`). Read the function, not the diff lines: what a
   change leaves the rest of the function to assume is where failures hide.
3. Wherever the code decides what happened (an outcome, a state, a record,
   what the person is told, whether work goes on), ask the question.
   - A person decided it: there is an entry in the expected-errors table for
     that named cause. Go to step 5.
   - Nobody decided it: the code is dealing with an unexpected error. Go to
     step 4.
4. For an unexpected error the rules allow almost no code, so the code is
   the finding. Two things only are allowed:
   - turning a failure that arrived as a value into a thrown error on the
     spot, keeping the other side's status, request id and error text, with
     no interpretation;
   - the one handler at the top of an entry point, which reports through the
     reporting function and tells the person "Something went wrong on our
     side", with nothing more specific.
   Everything else is a finding: work that goes on after a failure nobody
   decided on, a value or a sentence invented for it, a retry, a report call
   anywhere but the top handler, a failure recorded as a success, and the
   other side's status, request id or error text dropped on the way up. Also
   follow one failure up from each entry point the change touches and say
   whether it reaches a handler that reports it and tells the person.
5. Read every new or changed entry in the expected-errors tables, and every
   place that catches. Flag an entry whose cause is a status code, an
   exception type or "the request was not valid", an entry with no test, and
   an entry added without Kenneth's quoted yes in its commit message. Flag a
   catch that is neither recovering from an expected error nor translating
   at a boundary and rethrowing.
6. Report each finding as `file:line`, the rule it breaks, and what a person
   or the record would see go wrong. Say which findings you checked by
   running code and which only by reading. Code older than the range is not
   a finding of this audit; name it separately if it matters.

## Production check for a period

Input: a period in UTC. Use the service account, and a kubeconfig of your own
so the shared kubectl context does not change:

```bash

export KUBECONFIG=<scratch>/kubeconfig-tsd
gcloud container clusters get-credentials tsd --zone us-central1-c --project tsdtechnology
```

Deployment secrets (the Langfuse keys, the Sentry DSN) stay in memory: never
print them, never write them to a file or a message.

1. **Load balancer answers.** `scripts/lb_failures.py <from> <to>` lists every

The build session's work is deleted from both repositories, and that session is archived. Both folders now match their last commit, except for the rules text and the audit skill, which I kept. Nothing was committed, pushed or deployed.

## What was deleted

- **Desktop app:** 49 changed files restored to the last commit, and 6 new files removed. That covers the 17 report calls, the 50 written reasons on catch blocks, the reporting function, the expected-errors table, the catch-block scan and its workflow, and the release gating.
- **Server:** 12 changed files restored, and 3 new files removed. That covers the table of answers, the reporting to Sentry, the CircleCI test job, and the removal of the error-sentence setting from earlier today.
- **Before deleting,** I read every changed line in both repositories. All of it was that session's error-handling work, with no unrelated edits mixed in.

## What was kept

- **The rules text** in `AGENTS.md` (app) and `CLAUDE.md` (server), still uncommitted. I removed two things from each that pointed at deleted files: the sentence naming the table and the reporting function, and the bullet describing the check programs. In their place each file now says "This repository has no expected-errors table and no reporting function yet."
- **The audit skill.** I removed its step that ran the deleted checks, and corrected its production-check steps to describe what the server's committed code logs and sends.
- **A patch of everything deleted,** outside both repositories, in case any piece is wanted later: `/Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/error-sweep-trial/deleted-build-session-2026-11-15/`
- **Untouched:** the other untracked files in the app folder (release screenshots, design captures, a log file, a report) and the server's submodule.

One addition in the skill is my own wording, not something you approved: until a table exists, an auditor lists outcomes that look designed but have no entry separately from the other findings.

## What this leaves

- **The server is back to its old behavior.** It keeps only the status and request id of a provider failure, and reports only statuses 401, 403 and 404 to Sentry. "Keep the error sentence everywhere" applies when the reporting is rebuilt.
- **A reply that ends with the provider's own error is again recorded as completed.** That is one of the five known problems, and the deleted server code had addressed it.
- **Nothing was run after the deletion,** because the code is exactly the last commit. The local server still answers.

## Still waiting on you

The four decisions from my last message are unanswered: the rule clarification for tool calls, stack traces in reports, the route to Sentry, and whether a failing test stops a server release. The last one now has nothing behind it, since the test job is gone. The list of designed refusals outside AI requests is still owed by me, and I can now read it from clean code.

> Server, listed as unexpected and reported: “The request is not valid.”, “This model is not available.”, “This method is not allowed here.”, “The model service could not answer.”

Elaborate these. Why are they not expected? And under what kind of circumstances this will happen?

We don't need to show the whole stack. It'll be too overwhelming and too ugly for the users. Otherwise, I agree with you. We should just see in the stack when one exists. However, do double check to see if Sentry has a way to send C++ stack trace

to our own server, check to see if we already have a JustPrint Sentry project. If we don't, create one.

The uncommitted work runs the JusPrin tests beside the image build, so a failure shows red and the image is pushed anyway. My pick is that a failing test stops the image, since a test that stops nothing gets ignored. The cost is that a flaky test could hold up an urgent fix. Should a failure stop the image?

Now let's not let the test stop releases.

- **Adding a stack trace to an exception:** Sentry's docs say an exception created with `sentry_value_new_exception` has no stack trace and it must be added separately. The above exception does not contain a stack trace, which must be added separately. The Qt guide shows `sentry_value_set_stacktrace(exc, NULL, 0)` called on the exception before `sentry_event_add_exception` and `sentry_capture_event` (sentry_value_set_stacktrace(exc, NULL, 0);).

- **Event-level stack traces:** The Elaztek header mirror lists `sentry_event_value_add_stacktrace(event, ips, len)` as experimental and describes it as adding a stacktrace to an event. It also lists `sentry_unwind_stack` and `sentry_unwind_stack_from_ucontext` for capturing the instruction pointers (SENTRY_EXPERIMENTAL_API void sentry_event_value_add_stacktrace (sentry_value_t event, void **ips, size_t len)). This is a third-party copy of the header, so check the official headers for your version.

Removing the exception entry made the stack trace appear again. The thread in these results does not show a resolution (As soon as we set exception data, the stack trace for the event is corrupted).

- **C++ throws:** Another forum user on the 0.1.4 native SDK reported that when throwing C++ exceptions, the stack trace pointed to `sentry_crashpad.dll` instead of the throw site. Null-pointer crashes did not show this problem (I'm seeing the stacktrace in our sentry.io portal say that we are crashing in sentry_crashpad.dll).

You are a person who uses a desktop app for 3D printing called JusPrin. You are not a programmer and you know nothing about how the app is built. Look at three pictures of the app's screens and tell me, honestly, what you understand and what you do not. Do not read any other file, do not search the web, do not look at any code. Only open these three pictures with the Read tool:

1. /Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/work-error-report-2/renders/agent-ui-14-error-report-on-home.png
2. /Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/work-error-report-2/renders/agent-ui-15-error-report-at-sign-in.png
3. /Users/kenneth/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/work-error-report-2/renders/agent-ui-16-error-report-preferences.png

In each picture, ignore the bold heading and the grey sentence at the very top: those are notes for the designers and a real person never sees them. Judge only the app screen below them.

For each picture answer in plain sentences:
a. What do you think just happened, and how do you feel about it?
b. For every button, tick box, link and expandable line in the white window (pictures 1 and 2) or in the right-hand part of the page (picture 3): what do you expect to happen if you press or tick it? Say so even when you are unsure, and say that you are unsure.
c. What exactly would be sent, to whom, and when? Is anything sent if you do nothing?
d. Quote any word or sentence you had to read twice, found vague, or could not understand, and say why.
e. Anything that looks wrong, cut off, or out of place.

Then two questions across the pictures:
f. Suppose you ticked the box in picture 1 last week and now want to stop the automatic reports. Where would you go? Does picture 3 look like the place you expected, and does its page name fit?
g. In picture 1, one line says "Where: 9 lines naming the JusPrin code that was running". What do you think that means? Does it worry you?

Be specific and brief. Do not be polite about problems. If something is perfectly clear, say so in one line and move on.

Kenneth, 2026-11-15, on the two tables shown to him in chat: "This table looks good. Confirmed." The rule in AGENTS.md asks for his yes on every entry and his words in the commit message; these are the words. The code that held the tables was deleted the same day ([[desktop-app-error-reports-default-on]]); copies of the deleted files are in `error-sweep-trial/deleted-build-session-2026-11-15/`.

**Desktop app, failed AI requests** (cause → what the person sees → next step):
- App older than the server serves → "This version of JusPrin can no longer connect to JusPrin accounts." → Get the new version
- Sign-in ended, or own API key rejected → "Their sign-in has ended, or the API key was rejected." → Sign in again, or update the key
- Out of credits → "They are out of credits." → Get more credits
- Chat larger than the AI service accepts → "The request was too large for the AI service." → none shown today
- Provider or our server limiting speed → "The AI service is rate limited." → Wait, then Retry
- Provider overloaded → "The AI service is overloaded." → Wait, then Retry
- Provider down or unreachable from our server → "The AI service is temporarily unavailable." → Retry
- Provider too slow, or connection stalled → "The AI request timed out." → Retry
- No network → "The AI request could not reach the service." → Check the network, then Retry

**Server, expected answers:**
- Signed out → "Sign in to JusPrin to continue." → Sign in again
- Out of credits → "You do not have enough credits for this message." → Get more credits
- App too old → "This version of JusPrin can no longer connect to JusPrin accounts. Get the new version to keep using your account." → Get the new version
- Too many turns a minute, or provider limiting us → "Too many requests. Wait a moment and try again." → Wait and retry
- Server's slots for large requests all taken → "JusPrin is busy right now. Try again in a moment." → Retry
- Provider down, overloaded or unreachable → "The model service is unavailable. Try again shortly." → Retry
- Provider too slow → "The model service took too long to answer." → Retry
- Chat or report photos too large → "The request is too large." → New chat, or fewer pictures
- Print report too short → "A report needs a few sentences." → Write more
- Print report has no photo → "A report needs a photo of the printed object." → Add a photo
- Report photo cannot be opened → "That photo could not be read." → Add a different photo
- Print already reported → "This print already has a report." → Nothing

The second column is as shown to him: the app column is the build session's description of the sentence, not always the literal on-screen string, so check each against the code when rebuilding. Not confirmed, still his to judge: the server's four answers listed as unexpected (invalid_request, unknown_model, method_not_allowed, upstream_error) and the designed refusals outside AI requests (sign-in, attachments, import, print report).

content.text:
The boards are on the canvas, Sentry has a JusPrin project, and your decisions are recorded. Nothing is built, and no code changed this turn. Two things below need your call: where the Preferences box lives, and one point about tool-call failures.

## Boards

Four new boards sit in the error-report row of the "Agent UI · States & Components" page on the [canvas](https://claude.ai/artifact/ENCtdaz7gjynfbcy4JYbWJ). The pictures are attached above.

- **On Home:** the same dialog, in the middle of the window. The report is opened, and the stack appears as one line: "Where: 9 lines naming the parts of JusPrin that were running".
- **At sign-in:** the same dialog over the first-launch sign-in form.
- **The box:** "Report errors to the JusPrin team automatically", drawn twice, under Account and under Updates.

A first-time reader, shown only the pictures, said they would look for the box under Privacy, then Account, and never under Updates. Account also already carries the note on what JusPrin receives. So Account is my pick, and the dialog boards now say "Preferences › Account". I made changes after that reader's check and did not run a second check.

## Tool calls

You are right, and it is built. Each turn shows one collapsed line, such as "5 actions · 1 failed". Opened, a failed action carries a warning sign and the word "Failed", with the error underneath. The AI model also receives the error and carries on.

**Decision needed: should the app's own failure inside a tool call also be reported to us?** The activity line tells the person, but it tells us nothing.
- **Never report it.** Our own bugs in tools stay invisible to us.
- **Report it silently, only when automatic reports are on (my pick).** No dialog, because the turn usually recovers.
- **Open the dialog as for any other failure.** It interrupts a turn that is still going.

## The four server answers

Each is unexpected because only our own app talks to this server, so a refusal means one side has a bug.

- **"The request is not valid."** The app sent something the server will not accept: an unknown field, a missing header, a body that is not JSON. It is also what the server answers when the AI provider itself refuses a request with status 400. That second case is exactly the 29 failures of 2026-11-14.
- **"This model is not available."** The app asked for a model the server does not have. This would happen if we retire a model while a chat still uses it. I suggest designing that outcome on the day we retire one.
- **"This method is not allowed here."** Something other than the app's normal kind of request arrived. Only a bug or a person poking at the server does this.
- **"The model service could not answer."** The provider refused in a way nobody planned for, such as our own key being rejected, or the connection dropped mid-reply.

## Sentry

- **Project:** none existed, so I created `jusprin` on sentry.obico.io. Nothing sends to it yet.
- **C++ stacks:** Sentry can take them, in two ways. Its C++ library attaches the stack at the point where our code calls it. Or the app sends raw addresses through our server, and Sentry turns them into function names. Both need each release's debug files uploaded to Sentry. Both show where the failure was caught, not where it started, unless we record the stack at the moment of failure. I propose the first version sends stacks from the app's pages only, and C++ stacks come later.

## Recorded

- **The two tables:** confirmed, with your words kept for the commit message.
- **Releases:** tests do not stop them.

## Designed refusals outside AI requests

The list has 89 rows and is too long for chat: [designed-refusals-outside-ai-requests.md](designed-refusals-outside-ai-requests.md). It also flags problems, for example a second report of the same print shows "Report sent" with no explanation.

The sorted file is [designed-refusals-sorted.md](designed-refusals-sorted.md).

## The four piles

| Pile | Rows | What you need to do |
|---|---|---|
| Drawn on the design canvas, nothing found wrong | 28 | Nothing |
| Not drawn on any board, nothing found wrong | 28 | One decision, below |
| Wording or dead text | 8 | Nothing yet |
| The reader found something wrong | 17 | Nothing until they are reproduced |

"Drawn on the canvas" means a script found the sentence in one of the 253 canvas files. It does not prove you approved that board.

## The one decision

The 28 rows that no board draws are of two kinds.

- **Seventeen are real named causes**, such as "Too many codes were sent to this address. Try again in an hour." or "This G-code is no longer kept." I propose entering these in the table as they are when it is rebuilt.
- **Eleven are failures that were given a sentence of their own.** Examples: "JusPrin couldn't start signing in. Try again.", "The G-code couldn't be written to …", "Your projects couldn't be loaded. JusPrin will keep trying."

**Decision needed: what happens to those eleven?** Nobody named a cause for them; the code only knows that something failed.
- **They become unexpected errors (my pick).** The person sees "Something went wrong on our side" and the report dialog, and we hear about it. This is what the rules say for a failure nobody understands.
- **They keep their sentences.** The person gets slightly more specific words, and we never hear about the failure.

## The 17 rows where something looks wrong

All of these come from reading code. I checked five against the code: three match, and two I could only confirm in part. Examples:

- **Deleting an account** says "Check your internet connection" for every failure, whatever the cause.
- **A picture over 10 MiB** is accepted, and only the AI model is told it was too large. The person is told nothing.
- **A second report of the same print** shows "Report sent" with no credits and no explanation.
- **A server fault while signing in** is shown as "JusPrin couldn't be reached".
- **"Standard can't see pictures"** names Standard even when a different model is the one that cannot read pictures.
- **Eight developer-worded sentences**, such as "The packaged AI page is missing from this build.", are app faults and not refusals.

By your rule none of these gets a fix before it is reproduced. I put up a task card for a separate session to do only that: run the app, check each of the 17, and report which ones really happen. It fixes nothing. It starts only if you start it.

## The 8 wording rows

The outcome is right in each, but the words are a programmer's ("UTF-8", "FFF", "rebuild JusPrin"), or the sentence can never appear. I will draft replacements when the table is rebuilt.
